improvements: With guards should adopt Before guards's sharper playtest questions (first-minute discomfort, gait shortening, reaching for support) and a seated/PC fallback for unsteady walkers.
Before guards should convert one stop into a designed rest ritual with a staff-offered real chair, as With guards does at the tea stall.
Before guards should remove or reframe the hidden time-based scoring to fully honor the no-rush constraint.
Before guards's build plan should carry the prototype's sketch coordinates forward into per-checkpoint placement instructions, as With guards's does.

Both should reconcile the 'runner' genre label with the actual slow-tour experience, and both could specify text size/contrast thresholds (e.g., minimum letter height at reading distance) rather than just 'large high-contrast'.

summary: Both sessions converge on the same core design: a 6-player simultaneous MR walking race through a neon sci-fi course at Fortal court, with ordered checkpoints, red electrical-leak hazards that send you back to the last checkpoint, a 300-second limit, live leaderboard, and spectators on the long side. The key difference is spatial: Before guards builds two long lanes spanning the full 22 m court shared by all six players with 9 checkpoints, while With guards divides the court into a 2×3 grid of private 5.9 × 6.27 m cells, each containing a compact zigzag route with 8 checkpoints. With guards is more specific and internally consistent about space and safety (exact taping arithmetic, explicit "no shared-floor avatar play", no-void-floor instruction, per-hazard placement notes). Before guards better matches the brief's fantasy of racing through a course across the full court and gives richer pacing/story beats, but leaves the shared-space safety question less resolved (its own options step flags lane-crossing risk, and the build brief never states whether players share the floor or get copies). Both are feasible and well-aligned overall; With guards edges ahead on buildability and safety clarity, Before guards on brief fit and drama.
why: With guards wins on the things most likely to make or break the actual build: it resolves the 6-player physical layout with exact, verifiable arithmetic, explicitly states there is no shared-floor play (removing the collision ambiguity Before guards leaves open), gives per-hazard placement guidance that a builder can execute without further design decisions, and maintains tighter step-to-step consistency (8 checkpoints, 4 hazards, and scoring match exactly from options through prototype to build brief, including the sketch). Before guards is the more evocative design — full-court lanes better match the 'race through a course' fantasy and its pacing arc (mid-run twist, scenic pause, bridge climax) is richer — but its build brief never reconciles how 6 real bodies share 2 lanes across a 22 m court, which its own options step flagged as the top risk. Since the brief is for a real venue with real families watching, the safer, more buildable plan carries more weight, and With guards delivers that without sacrificing the core fun. The margin is modest because Before guards is genuinely stronger on concept fit and drama.

differences.aspect: Use of the venue and fit to the 'race through a course' concept
differences.with_rag: A compact zigzag inside a private 5.9 × 6.27 m cell per player, duplicated 2×3 across the court (build brief: 'Use a compact two-lane zigzag inside each cell, not a course spanning the full court'). Each player covers much less ground and the route folds back on itself.
differences.without_rag: Two long lanes spanning the full 22 m court with 9 checkpoints spaced ~2.5–9 m apart (options step: 'use the 22 m length of the indoor court for two long lanes'; build brief: 'two long, gently bending lanes spanning the full 22 m court'). This delivers the brief's fantasy of running through a course across the whole space.
differences.evidence: Before guards build brief: 'two long, gently bending lanes spanning the full 22 m court; the lanes must never cross'. With guards build brief: 'Design the route for ONE cell measuring 5.9 x 6.27 m, then duplicate it into a 2 x 3 grid... not a course spanning the full court'.

differences.aspect: Player separation and collision safety clarity
differences.with_rag: Explicitly resolves this: 'each walking an identical private copy of the Land; there is no shared-floor avatar play', with exact taping arithmetic (0.6 + 5.9 + 1 + 5.9 + 0.6 = 14 m; 0.6 + 6.27 + 1 + 6.27 + 1 + 6.27 + 0.6 = 22 m), 1 m gaps between cells, and 'Do not route players across cell gaps or into another player's copy'.
differences.without_rag: Options step says all 6 players 'still share the real space' and lists 'must separate start positions and control lane-cutting or running' as a risk; prototype adds separated spawns, ≥1.2 m corridors, no lane-cutting. But the final build brief never states whether players share one floor or each get a copy, and with 6 players on 2 lanes spanning 22 m the physical arrangement of 6 bodies is never resolved.
differences.evidence: Before guards options risks: 'ผู้เล่น 6 คนยังใช้พื้นที่จริงร่วมกัน ต้องแยกตำแหน่งเริ่มและควบคุมไม่ให้ตัดเลนหรือเร่งวิ่ง' (6 players still share the real space; must separate starts and prevent lane-cutting/running). With guards build brief: 'there is no shared-floor avatar play... Copy this taping arithmetic exactly'.

differences.aspect: Specificity and actionability of the build brief
differences.with_rag: Build brief is more prescriptive: exact cell dimensions and grid arithmetic, per-checkpoint placement descriptions tied to route segments, per-hazard placement notes (H1 'on the straight well before its turn... generous clearance', H2 'one deliberate sidestep', H3 'never hide it behind the tower', H4 'separated from both checkpoint 7 and the final turn'), explicit 'Do not use a void floor', and color hex codes with a non-glow readability requirement.
differences.without_rag: Build brief gives checkpoint count (9), spacing range (2.5–9 m), Thai labels per checkpoint, hazard density guidance per segment, corridor width, wall/door clearances, and spectator-side placement of the climax. Solid but leaves exact geometry to the builder.
differences.evidence: With guards build brief hazard section: 'H3... Increase pressure through placement, not surprise; never hide it behind the tower' and 'Do not use a void floor'. Before guards build brief gives no per-hazard placement beyond density guidance between checkpoint ranges.

differences.with_rag: Prototype also has a pause (after checkpoint 5) and a climactic final hazard H4 near spectators, but the arc is flatter: hazards are just 4 discrete circles, the 'shortcut gates' are thematically thin (they frame the route but don't function as shortcuts), and the story (restore the city's power) is similar but less developed.
differences.without_rag: Prototype defines a clear difficulty arc with a story twist (checkpoint 3: the energy abyss starts swallowing the city), a scenic hazard-free pause at checkpoint 7, and a climax on a visually narrow bridge over the abyss with two hazard groups before the finish; flow timestamps map the full 5 minutes.
differences.evidence: Before guards flow: '1:15 ถึงจุดตรวจ 3... หลุมพลังงานเริ่มกลืนแท่นเมือง' (checkpoint 3 twist: abyss starts swallowing platforms) and '3:15 จุดตรวจ 7 เป็นช่วงพักสั้นไม่มีอันตราย' (hazard-free scenic pause). With guards flow has a pause at 3:30 and climax at 4:00–4:20 but the build brief describes shortcut gates as 'frames the onward route but does not obstruct it' with no mechanical effect.

differences.with_rag: Very consistent: 8 checkpoints with the same breakdown (3 cores, 2 shortcut gates, 2 towers, 1 portal), 4 hazards, scoring, 300 s, cell dimensions, and even the sketch's 4 danger zones match H1–H4 in the build brief. The prototype's 'no void floor' concern (decision about not relying on glow, easy first round) is reflected in the build brief.
differences.without_rag: Mostly consistent: 9 checkpoints, scoring (+100/−25/+300), 5-minute limit, spectator-side climax all carry through. Minor drift: options step says hazard penalty is returning to last checkpoint with no score mention, prototype adds −25; options mention 'two lanes' for the route which persists but the 6-player physical arrangement is never reconciled.
differences.evidence: With guards prototype decisions list '8 ด่าน... ปลดล็อกแกนพลังงาน 3 จุด ประตูทางลัด 2 จุด หอส่งสัญญาณ 2 จุด และเปิดพอร์ทัล 1 จุด' and the build brief places exactly these 8 with matching labels; sketch zones include exactly 4 danger zones matching H1–H4. Before guards options vs prototype: penalty rule gains −25 points only at prototype stage.

differences.with_rag: Same plan: H4 climactic dodge and portal on the spectator-facing side, wall leaderboard, cheering/calling rankings. Key art prompt also includes families along the long side. Functionally equivalent.
differences.without_rag: Final two hazard groups, checkpoint 9, and finish portal placed near the long spectator side; wall leaderboard; spectators can cheer or call out the next checkpoint. Key art prompt explicitly includes 'real families watching safely beyond the long sideline'.
differences.evidence: Before guards spectator_plan: 'จะได้เห็นช่วงหลบกระแสไฟสองชุดบนสะพานท้ายเกมและการเข้าประตูเมืองอย่างชัดเจน' (clear view of the two bridge hazard groups and gate entry). With guards spectator_plan: 'จะเห็นจังหวะหลบวงกระแสไฟสุดท้ายและการเดินเข้าพอร์ทัลได้ชัดเจน' (clear view of the final hazard dodge and portal entry).

differences.with_rag: Explicitly acknowledges the trade-off: options risk states 'everyone sees their own course, doesn't walk on a shared floor or see friends' avatars; group feeling relies on cheering and the leaderboard'. Players see real bodies in adjacent cells but no shared virtual space.
differences.without_rag: Fellowship comes from racing simultaneously, cheering, and comparing scores; players presumably see each other's real bodies on the shared court (implied by shared-space risk note), which adds social presence.
differences.evidence: With guards options risks: 'ทุกคนเห็นสนามของตัวเอง ไม่ได้เดินบนพื้นร่วมหรือเห็นอวตารเพื่อน ความเป็นกลุ่มจึงพึ่งเสียงเชียร์และลีดเดอร์บอร์ด' (no shared floor or avatars; fellowship depends on cheers and leaderboard). Before guards implies co-presence but never confirms it.

differences.with_rag: Same three genres (runner, sword, chess) with similar scoring. With guards's options include more concrete numbers earlier (cell size 5.9 × 6.27 m, board 6×8 with 0.70 m squares) and the chess option honestly scores fun at 3 for mismatch with the running fantasy.
differences.without_rag: Three options: the runner (recommended), a chess-tactics game, and a sword battle game. Each option includes honest self-scores and explicit risks; the sword option even recommends dropping to 2–3 players per round if space is insufficient.
differences.evidence: Before guards option 3 risk: 'หากจัดแน่นเกินไปควรลดจำนวนรอบละ 2–3 คน' (if too crowded, reduce to 2–3 players per round). With guards option 3 scores: fun 3 with 'จังหวะคิดไม่ตรงกับแฟนตาซีการวิ่งผ่านด่าน' (thinking pace doesn't match the running-through-course fantasy).

with_rag_weaknesses: The compact 5.9 × 6.27 m zigzag cells mean each player covers far less ground and the route folds back on itself, weakening the brief's fantasy of racing through a course across the venue.

The 'shortcut gates' (checkpoints 3 and 5) are thematically named but mechanically inert — the build brief says they 'frame the onward route but do not obstruct it', so they don't function as shortcuts.
Flatter dramatic arc: only 4 discrete hazard circles and no mid-run story twist; the pause after checkpoint 5 is functional rather than scenic.
Fellowship is explicitly weaker by design — no shared floor or friend avatars — relying entirely on cheering and the leaderboard.
without_rag_weaknesses: The final build brief never states whether the 6 players share one physical floor or each get a copy, despite the options step flagging shared-space lane-crossing as the top risk — the physical arrangement of 6 bodies on 2 lanes is unresolved.
Slightly less prescriptive build brief: hazard placement is given only as density guidance between checkpoint ranges, with no per-hazard placement or clearance notes.
